title: Bridges and tests: callbackFlow, Reactor and runTest
goal: By the end you can wrap a listener API in callbackFlow without leaking the listener or losing events, predict how Reactor demand and Flow suspension map onto each other, give Java callers a Flux, and test flows on virtual time knowing what runCurrent, advanceTimeBy, advanceUntilIdle and Turbine show and hide.

warmup.q: A test runs `backgroundScope.launch { gateway.events().collect { got += it } }`, where `events()` is a correct `callbackFlow` that registers a listener, and on the very next line calls `gateway.fire(event)`. Then it calls `runCurrent()`. What is in `got`?
options: Nothing: the listener wasn't registered when the event fired
warmup.why: On the default `StandardTestDispatcher`, `launch` only queues the collector. The `callbackFlow` block that calls `register` runs in a producer coroutine when the scheduler next runs, which is at `runCurrent()`, after the fire. The event found no listener and went nowhere. Production code has the same gap.

sections.h: A burst of 200: 64 slots and one waiting hand
sections.body:
On connect, many SDKs replay what you missed in one synchronous burst. Fire 200 events into a default `callbackFlow` while its collector waits in `receive()`, and 135 `trySend` calls fail. The other 65 got through: 64 into the channel's buffer (`Channel.BUFFERED`), and one handed straight to the receiver that was already waiting, before the buffer was touched. So a buffer of 64 accepts 65 when a receiver is waiting. Better to know that before a test counts it for you.

`trySend` returns a `ChannelResult`. Ignore it, and the 135 failures are silent loss. After the channel is closed it fails too, with `isClosed=true`. The fix is a policy you choose on purpose. A `buffer(...)` or `conflate()` right after `callbackFlow { }` is fused into its one channel (lesson 4 of this track), so it changes that channel instead of adding a second one:

| After `callbackFlow { }` | `trySend` failures | The collector got |
|---|---|---|
| nothing (64, `SUSPEND`) | 135 | 65 accepted |
| `.buffer(Channel.UNLIMITED)` | 0 | all 200 |
| `.conflate()` | 0 | `[0, 199]`: the first went to the waiting receiver, the last stayed in the one slot |
| `.buffer(10, DROP_OLDEST)` | 0 | `[0, 190, 191, ..., 199]` |

```kotlin
fun DemoGateway.events(): Flow<PayEvent> = callbackFlow { /* register, trySend, awaitClose */ }
    .buffer(500)   // fused: the bridge's own channel now holds the documented 500-event replay
```

```java
// Java equivalent: Flux.create buffers without limit by default (OverflowStrategy.BUFFER);
// onBackpressureBuffer(500) caps it and fails with an overflow error past 500
Flux<PayEvent> events = Flux.create(sink -> { /* register, sink.next, onDispose */ })
    .onBackpressureBuffer(500);
```

`trySendBlocking(e)` looks like the safe version. It is `trySend` with a fallback of `runBlocking { send(e) }`, so when the buffer is full it blocks the SDK's own thread until there is room. With an SDK thread pushing 200 events and a collector that takes 2 ms each, `trySend` let the thread finish at once and lost 135, while `trySendBlocking` lost none and held the SDK thread for about 300 ms. (That run is real time, so your numbers will differ.) Use it only when the SDK runs your callback on a worker thread of its own and blocking that thread is how you push back. Pick `UNLIMITED` only when the producer is bounded. For a feed where only the latest status matters, `conflate()` drops in a way you can explain.

sections.h: Across the Reactor bridge, demand becomes suspension
sections.body:
Reactive Streams makes the subscriber say how much it can take, with `request(n)`. A Flow has no such call: it suspends. The bridges in kotlinx-coroutines-reactive and -reactor translate one into the other.

`Publisher.asFlow()` works like a diner with an order pad. It requests 64, eats them, then requests 64 more after every 64 it has passed downstream. (A `Flux` is a `Publisher`, so `flux.asFlow()` is this same function.) The elements wait in a channel of that size, and `buffer` sets the size of the order:

| Flow side | Requests sent to a 300-item `Flux` |
|---|---|
| `asFlow()` | 64 after 0, 64, 128, 192 and 256 |
| `asFlow().buffer(10)` | 10 every 10 |
| `asFlow().buffer(0)` | 1 every 1 |
| `asFlow().conflate()` or `.buffer(UNLIMITED)` | `Long.MAX_VALUE`, once |
| `asFlow().take(3)` | 64, then cancel: the 61 extra already in the channel are thrown away |

That is a batch refill. Reactor's own operators top up earlier: `publishOn` asked a Flow-backed Flux for 256 and then 192 at a time, and `limitRate(10)` for 10 and then 8.

`Flow.asFlux()` and `asPublisher()` go the other way. Nothing runs until the first `request(n)`. Then each `emit` calls `onNext` right there, inside `emit`, and counts the demand down. When it reaches 0, the flow suspends inside that `emit`, and a later `request` resumes it. After `request(2)` the subscriber had `[1, 2]`, and `emit` had returned only for 1: the flow was parked inside `emit(2)`. Cancelling the subscription cancels the flow's coroutine, so a `callbackFlow` underneath runs its `awaitClose`.

Two details bite in production. The bridge runs the flow on `Dispatchers.Unconfined` unless you pass a dispatcher, so the flow and every Reactor operator after it run on whichever thread resumed it: the subscriber's thread at first, `kotlinx.coroutines.DefaultExecutor` after a `delay`, and the SDK's own thread under a gateway bridge. Pass `asFlux(dispatcher)` or add `publishOn` before anything slow downstream. And Reactor's `Context` crosses in both directions. Through `asFlux()`, a `traceId` written with `contextWrite` was visible inside the flow as a `ReactorContext` element. The other way, a `ReactorContext` in the coroutine reaches a publisher collected with `asFlow()` only when kotlinx-coroutines-reactor is on the classpath, because that module supplies the injector, found with `ServiceLoader`.

Java can't call `Flow.collect`, which it sees as `Object collect(FlowCollector, Continuation)`. Give Java a face built in Kotlin:

```kotlin
class GatewayApi(private val gateway: FakeGateway) {
    fun events(): Flow<GatewayEvent> = gateway.events()        // for Kotlin callers
    fun eventsFlux(): Flux<GatewayEvent> = events().asFlux()   // for Java and Reactor callers
}
```

```java
// Java caller: only Reactor types, no Flow and no Continuation
List<GatewayEvent> firstTwo = new GatewayApi(gateway).eventsFlux().take(2).collectList().block();
```

For a finite result, a `CompletableFuture` built with `scope.future { }` is the better face, as lesson 11 of the coroutines track showed.

Part 3: `[PENDING, CAPTURED]` for the Standard collector and `[PENDING, AUTHORIZED, CAPTURED]` for the Unconfined one. sections.h: Turbine is a stenographer, and it hears everything
sections.body:
Turbine 1.2.1 (`app.cash.turbine`, a test dependency of this lab module) turns a flow into a transcript you read line by line:

```kotlin
gateway.events().test {          // collects before the block runs: the listener is registered
    gateway.fire(authorized)
    assertThat(awaitItem()).isEqualTo(authorized)
    gateway.fail(IOException("gateway connection lost"))
    assertThat(awaitError()).hasMessage("gateway connection lost")
}
```

```java
// Java equivalent: StepVerifier subscribes, then runs each step in order
StepVerifier.create(api.eventsFlux())
    .then(() -> gateway.fire(authorized))
    .expectNext(authorized)
    .then(() -> gateway.fail(new IOException("gateway connection lost")))
    .expectErrorMessage("gateway connection lost")
    .verify(Duration.ofSeconds(5));
```

Picture a court stenographer. `test { }` runs the flow up to its first suspension before your block starts, so a SharedFlow is subscribed and a `callbackFlow` listener is registered by then, which removes the race from the first section. Every event goes into the transcript, an unlimited channel, in order. You read it with `awaitItem()`, `awaitComplete()` and `awaitError()`, which hands you the error as an event instead of throwing it. An event you never read fails the test with `Unconsumed events found`, unless you end with `cancelAndIgnoreRemainingEvents()`. If no new line arrives within 3 s of wall-clock time, the test fails with `No value produced in 3s`. The flow's own `delay` calls stay virtual inside `runTest`; only Turbine's wait is real. To follow two flows at once, call `testIn(backgroundScope)` inside `turbineScope { }`. Outside it, `testIn` compiles and then fails at run time with `Turbine can only collect flows within a TurbineContext`.

The stenographer hears everything, and that is its blind spot. Turbine collects on `UnconfinedTestDispatcher`, so it takes each value the instant it is sent. It saw AUTHORIZED, which the Standard collector of the last section never got. It also took all 500 events of a burst through a 64-slot `callbackFlow`, where a Standard collector got 65. Use Turbine to check what a flow emits and in what order. Don't use it to test conflation, buffer sizes or a slow consumer. For those, collect with a Standard collector in `backgroundScope` and drive the clock yourself, as the lab's burst test does. And on a SharedFlow with no replay, a value emitted before `test { }` starts is gone, so the test fails with `No value produced`.

refs.title: Testing Kotlin flows (Android developers): the StateFlow conflation warning

analogy: A `callbackFlow` is a mailbox bolted to an SDK's front door. The SDK's van drops letters through the slot with `trySend`; the box holds 64, and one more goes straight into a hand that is already waiting. `awaitClose` is you on the porch, ready to unscrew the box when you're told to leave. The Reactor bridge is a restaurant order pad: the Kotlin diner orders 64 plates and orders again after eating 64, while Reactor's waiter orders n, and the Kotlin cook serves each plate the moment it is ready and stops mid-motion when the order runs out. The test scheduler is a film editor's timeline with the empty stretches cut, and Turbine is a stenographer who writes down every word. The analogy breaks at the stenographer. A real one can only write as fast as people speak, but Turbine takes every value the instant it is sent, which is why it can't show you what a slower listener would miss.
in_your_world: Most payment SDKs you wrap have a listener API: a card-gateway client with `onEvent` and `onError`, a webhook dispatcher, a settlement-file watcher. Each becomes a `callbackFlow` with `awaitClose` and a buffer sized for the burst its documentation promises on reconnect, with failed `trySend` results counted in a metric so that a loss is visible. When Java code in the same Quarkus or Spring application calls that Kotlin service, give it a `Flux` built with `asFlux()` (with a dispatcher if the operators after it are slow, because otherwise they run on the SDK's thread) or a `CompletableFuture` for a finite answer, and never a `Flow`. In the tests, inject the dispatcher, wait for the registration before firing events, collect hot flows in `backgroundScope`, and keep Turbine for content and order, with a Standard collector for anything about timing or buffers.
mistake: The most common mistake is a `callbackFlow` test that fires an event right after launching the collector: `backgroundScope.launch { gateway.events().collect { got += it } }`, then `gateway.fire(event)`. On the default `StandardTestDispatcher` the collector hasn't run, its producer hasn't registered, and the event goes nowhere; afterwards `got` is empty and the listener count is 1. People then add a `delay` or switch every test to Unconfined, and the second fix can hide a buffer that is too small. Make the registration explicit instead: call `runCurrent()` after the launch and assert the listener count, or use Turbine's `test { }`, which registers before its block runs. Production has the same gap, so code that fires events right after it starts collecting needs its own signal that the listener is in place.

compare.title: A gateway bridge: Flux.create next to callbackFlow

java.title: GatewayEvents.java (Reactor)

kotlin.title: GatewayEvents.kt (callbackFlow)

compare.note: The shapes match line for line, and four things differ. Registration time: `Flux.create` registers inside `subscribe()`, while `callbackFlow` registers when its producer coroutine first runs, so an event fired right after `collect` starts can be lost. Cleanup: `callbackFlow` throws when its block returns without `awaitClose`, and Reactor lets a missing `onDispose` leak the listener with no message. Buffering: Kotlin's channel holds 64 (65 with a waiting receiver) and makes you look at `trySend`'s result; Reactor buffers without limit unless you add a policy. Threads: `sink.next` calls the subscriber's `onNext` on the SDK's thread, while the Kotlin collector runs on its own dispatcher and the SDK thread only drops the event into the channel. That holds until you turn the flow into a Flux with plain `asFlux()`, whose `Unconfined` default puts the subscriber back on the SDK's thread.

steps: Run the tests. The five `GatewayEventsTest` cases and the three in `GatewayFluxTest` (a Java test) fail. `TurbineTourTest` and `StepVerifierTourTest` already pass: they are this lesson's Try it. Read one failure: it is the `awaitClose` message from the first section.

hints: `close(error)` and `close()` belong to the `ProducerScope` the block runs in, so you can call them from inside the listener object.

`Expected size: 500 but was: 65` is the default 64 slots plus the one event handed to the waiting collector. A `buffer(...)` right after `callbackFlow { }` is fused into its channel. `Channel.UNLIMITED` passes too; a number states how much memory you allow.
Don't reach for `trySendBlocking`. In the burst test the SDK's thread is the test's only thread, the one the collector needs in order to run.

drill.title: A listener bridge, from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. A made-up webhook SDK has `fun subscribe(onDelivery: (Delivery) -> Unit, onFailure: (Throwable) -> Unit): Cancellable`. Write `fun WebhookSdk.deliveries(): Flow<Delivery>` that never blocks the SDK's thread, fails the flow on `onFailure`, holds a burst of 1,000 deliveries, and cancels the SDK subscription whatever ends the collection. Then say in a comment what happens if you leave out the cleanup line.

alt.title: Java equivalent

recap: `callbackFlow` registers when its producer coroutine first runs, after `collect` starts, so an event fired in between is lost. Tests wait for the registration; Turbine's `test { }` does it for you. Reactor's `Flux.create` registers inside `subscribe()`.

`awaitClose { unregister() }` runs on `take(n)`, cancellation, `close(error)` and `close()`. Without it, collecting throws the exact `IllegalStateException` shown in the lesson. Use `channelFlow` for your own coroutines and `suspendCancellableCoroutine` for a one-shot callback.

The bridge holds 64 by default plus one handed to a waiting receiver, so 65 of a 200-event burst got in. Check `trySend`'s result, and choose a fused `buffer(n)`, `conflate()` or `UNLIMITED` (for a bounded producer) on purpose. `trySendBlocking` blocks the SDK's thread.

`Publisher.asFlow()` requests 64, then 64 more after each 64; `buffer(n)` makes it `request(n)`. `asFlux()` starts at the first request, calls `onNext` inside `emit` and suspends there when demand runs out, on `Unconfined` unless you pass a dispatcher. Give Java a `Flux` or a `CompletableFuture`, never a `Flow`.

`advanceTimeBy(n)` runs what is due before `now + n`, `runCurrent()` what is due now, and `advanceUntilIdle()` stops when only `backgroundScope` work is left. A Standard collector shows StateFlow conflation; an Unconfined one shows every value.

Turbine reads a flow like a transcript with a 3 s wall-clock timeout. It collects on `UnconfinedTestDispatcher`, so it can't show conflation or a buffer that is too small: test those with a Standard collector and the clock.

quiz.q: A `callbackFlow` with the default buffer is followed by `.conflate()`. Its collector is suspended, waiting for the first element, when the SDK fires events 0 to 199 synchronously. What does the collector get?
options: `[0, 199]`: the first went straight to the waiting collector, the last stayed in the one slot
quiz.why: `conflate()` is fused into the callbackFlow's channel and turns it into one slot that a new element overwrites. Event 0 was handed directly to the receiver that was already waiting, so it never touched the slot; the slot then ended up holding 199. Lesson 4's `conflate()` works the same way.

quiz.q: A test runs `backgroundScope.launch { gateway.events().collect { got += it } }`, then `gateway.fire(e)` on the next line, then `runCurrent()`. `events()` is a correct `callbackFlow` with `awaitClose`. What are `got` and the listener count afterwards?
options: `[]` and 1: the listener registered after the fire
quiz.why: The default `StandardTestDispatcher` only queues the collector. Its producer coroutine, which calls `register`, runs at `runCurrent()`, after the fire, so the event found no listener; from then on one listener is registered. Call `runCurrent()` before firing, or use Turbine's `test { }`.

quiz.q: Reactor code subscribes to `ledger.asFlux()`, where `ledger = flow { for (i in 1..10) { emit(i); log += i } }`, with a subscriber that calls `request(2)` and nothing more. What has the subscriber received, and what is in `log`?
options: Nothing yet: the flow waits for `request(64)`
`[1, 2]` and `[1]`: the flow is suspended inside `emit(2)`
quiz.why: `asFlux()` calls `onNext` inside `emit` and then counts the demand down. After the second `onNext` the demand is 0, so the flow suspends inside `emit(2)` before `log += 2` runs. A later `request(n)` resumes it. The 64 is the other direction: `Publisher.asFlow()` requests 64 at a time.

quiz.q: `authorizeAndCapture()` sets a StateFlow to AUTHORIZED and then CAPTURED with no suspension between. Which test setup can show that a collector misses AUTHORIZED?
options: `backgroundScope.launch { status.toList(seen) }` on the default dispatcher, with `runCurrent()` before and after
quiz.why: Only a Standard collector waits for its turn, so it wakes to CAPTURED and records `[PENDING, CAPTURED]`. Turbine and the Unconfined collector run inside each set and see all three. `take(3)` waits for a third value that never comes and fails with `UncompletedCoroutinesError`.

quiz.q: From lesson 7 of this track: request handlers read `rates.value` from `feed.stateIn(appScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), null)` and never collect. What do they read?
options: `null` for ever: reading `.value` is not a subscription, so the feed never starts
The first rate, and never an update
quiz.why: `WhileSubscribed` starts the upstream from `subscriptionCount`, and `.value` doesn't count as a subscriber. Nothing ever starts the feed. A cache read through `.value` needs `Eagerly` or the suspend `stateIn(scope)`.

flashcards.front: When does a `callbackFlow` register its listener?
flashcards.back: When its producer coroutine first runs, after collection starts. An event fired before that is lost. Reactor's `Flux.create` registers inside `subscribe()`.

flashcards.front: What happens when a `callbackFlow` block returns without `awaitClose`?
flashcards.back: Collecting throws `IllegalStateException: 'awaitClose { yourCallbackOrListener.cancel() }' should be used in the end of callbackFlow block.`

flashcards.front: A collector waits on a default `callbackFlow`, and the SDK fires 200 events synchronously. How many `trySend` calls succeed?
flashcards.back: 65: 64 buffered, plus 1 handed straight to the waiting receiver. The other 135 fail, and are lost unless you check the result.

flashcards.front: How does `Publisher.asFlow()` request from the publisher?
flashcards.back: `request(64)`, then 64 more after every 64 collected. `buffer(n)` makes it `request(n)`; `conflate()` and `UNLIMITED` request `Long.MAX_VALUE`.

flashcards.front: With `asFlux()`, where does the flow suspend when the subscriber's demand runs out?
flashcards.back: Inside `emit`, right after the `onNext` that used the last of the demand. A later `request(n)` resumes it.

flashcards.front: Tasks are due at +100 and +200 ms. What does `advanceTimeBy(100)` run?
flashcards.back: Nothing: it runs tasks due before now + 100 and leaves the clock at 100. `runCurrent()` then runs the task at 100.

flashcards.front: Why can't a Turbine test show StateFlow conflation or a buffer that is too small?
flashcards.back: Turbine collects on `UnconfinedTestDispatcher` and takes every value the instant it is sent, so it sees all values and the buffer never fills.

terms.plain: A flow builder for listener APIs. Its block registers a listener that sends into a channel, and `awaitClose` removes the listener when the flow ends.
Suspends the `callbackFlow` block until its channel is closed, then runs your cleanup, whatever ended the flow.
In Reactive Streams, the number of items a subscriber has asked for with `request(n)` and not yet received.
A `buffer`, `conflate` or `flowOn` placed right after a channel-based flow changes that flow's own channel instead of adding a second one.
The test scheduler's clock in `runTest`. It jumps to the next due task, so a `delay` takes no real time.
A scope inside `runTest` for coroutines that never end. They are cancelled when the test body ends, and `advanceUntilIdle()` doesn't wait for them.
A test library (`app.cash.turbine`) that collects a flow into a queue you read with `awaitItem`, `awaitComplete` and `awaitError`.

explain_back.prompt: Explain to a teammate why `gateway.fire(e)` right after `backgroundScope.launch { gateway.events().collect { ... } }` loses the event in a test, why rewriting the test with Turbine fixes that, and why Turbine would then hide a buffer that is too small.
explain_back.answer: On the default StandardTestDispatcher, launch only queues the collector. The callbackFlow's producer coroutine, which calls register, runs the next time the scheduler runs, so the fire happens with no listener and the event goes nowhere. Turbine's test { } runs the flow up to its first suspension before the block starts, so by then the listener is registered. But Turbine collects on UnconfinedTestDispatcher. Each trySend resumes it at once and the event leaves the channel right away, so the channel never fills, and a 64-slot buffer passes a 500-event burst. To test the buffer, collect with a Standard collector that can't run during the burst: launch it, call runCurrent() so it registers, fire the burst, call runCurrent() again and count.

deeper.body:
The JDK has its own Reactive Streams interfaces, `java.util.concurrent.Flow`, with `Publisher`, `Subscriber` and `Subscription`. kotlinx.coroutines bridges them in a separate artifact, `org.jetbrains.kotlinx:kotlinx-coroutines-jdk9:1.11.0`. It is a thin wrapper over the reactive module: `asFlow()`, `asPublisher()` and `collect` for the JDK types, with the same demand mapping (a JDK publisher over 150 items saw `request(64)` three times). You don't need the extra artifact. reactive-streams 1.0.4, already on this lab's classpath through kotlinx-coroutines-reactive, has `org.reactivestreams.FlowAdapters`, and `FlowAdapters.toPublisher(jdkPublisher).asFlow()` does the same job.

The JDK `HttpClient` shows why that matters. `client.sendAsync(request, BodyHandlers.ofPublisher())` is two bridges in one call. The `CompletableFuture` completes once, when the headers arrive, so it belongs to `await()`. The body is a JDK `Flow.Publisher<List<ByteBuffer>>` that delivers chunks as they come off the socket, so it belongs to `asFlow()`. In one run against a local server that wrote five lines 50 ms apart, the chunks arrived about 50 ms apart too. Wrapping the future in `callbackFlow` would be the wrong tool: a single result is a `suspendCancellableCoroutine` or `await()` job.

A few facts about the Reactor modules themselves. The README of kotlinx-coroutines-reactive calls `asPublisher` TCK-compliant. The subscription it creates has no parent job, so its lifetime belongs to the subscription and not to any scope. Element types must be non-null (`T : Any`), because Reactive Streams forbids `null` items. And the 1.11.0 reactor module declares reactor-core 3.4.1 in its pom; this course pins 3.8.8, and Gradle picks the higher version.
